title: The best water filter pitchers and dispensers in the US, tested in a lab – and none are Brita
summary:

Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things Mikita Hill-Cashaw, Rachel Sherman , Alessandra Mora and Jonathan Deutsch Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jump to: Why you should trust us How we tested The best water filter systems in 2026 Water quality scores based on third-party lab testing What you need to know about water filter pitchers All the filters we tested W e have all had the experience of drinking water and thinking, “Oh ... that’s not right.” A water filter can help with the taste and much more – and a better understanding of them can help you pick the right one for daily use. Water quality can be affected by plumbing, geography, mineral buildup, weather events and emerging contaminants such as Pfas, pharmaceuticals and disinfection byproducts. Many filters on the market claim to remove impurities, but that doesn’t mean the technology is reducing the contaminants that you should be most concerned about. We decided to put these claims to the test. We tested nine different water filters for taste and ease of use, then third-party tested them in labs to evaluate their efficacy. Fascinatingly, the household-favorite Brita was beaten by many other brands. Why you should trust us We are students, professors and researchers from the Drexel Food Lab at Drexel University, a food product design and culinary innovation lab. For the Filter US, we have previously tested the best air fryers , the best nontoxic cookware and the best instant coffee , and answered common questions about food safety . How we tested View image in fullscreen We tested nine filters against a control sample from the Drexel Food Lab’s kitchen sink. Photograph: Mikita Hill-Cashaw/The Guardian We talked to public health experts and water quality engineers about how to choose the best water filter systems. After setting up each individual water filter using manufacturer instructions, we organized a blind taste test. Between 67 testers, we managed three rounds of tests in an elimination method. Winners move on; losers are left behind. We tested nine separate filters against a control sample from our lab’s kitchen sink. Each filter was assigned a randomized number, and participants were asked to smell and taste each sample in a random order Last, we sent samples to third-party labs facilitated by the water testing company Tap Score , using their Essential City Water Test and VOC Water Test, which were tested in labs in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, respectively. VOC stands for volatile organic compounds , or the toxic chemicals you don’t want in your water. We tested these water filters in our food lab in a commercial building on Drexel’s campus and our plumbing and water system is different from a residential setup. After sending our water to Tap Score for testing, we learned that our regular tap water has high quantities of chloroform and other water disinfection byproducts. These contaminants are a result of the chlorination process used to reduce bacteria in our drinking water. Your residential water should not be testing nearly as high as ours, but it does make you think about water quality for those who work from an office or industrial building.
